claim: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a muscular dystrophy caused by inefficient epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array and somatic expression of the DUX4 retrogene.
source: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a muscular dystrophy caused by inefficient epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array and somatic expression of the DUX4 retrogene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FSHD pathogenesis, supported by citations in the main text.

claim: DUX4 is a double homeobox transcription factor that is normally expressed in the testis.
source: DUX4 is a double homeobox transcription factor that is normally expressed in the testis and causes apoptosis and FSHD when misexpressed in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DUX4 expression pattern.

claim: DUX4 causes apoptosis and FSHD when misexpressed in skeletal muscle.
source: DUX4 is a double homeobox transcription factor that is normally expressed in the testis and causes apoptosis and FSHD when misexpressed in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the main text to previous studies.

claim: DUX4-triggered proteolytic degradation of UPF1 is associated with profound NMD inhibition.
source: We report that DUX4-triggered proteolytic degradation of UPF1, a central component of the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) machinery, is associated with profound NMD inhibition, resulting in global accumulation of RNAs normally degraded as NMD substrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing UPF1 degradation and accumulation of NMD substrates in DUX4-expressing cells.

claim: DUX4 expression results in global accumulation of RNAs normally degraded as NMD substrates.
source: We report that DUX4-triggered proteolytic degradation of UPF1, a central component of the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) machinery, is associated with profound NMD inhibition, resulting in global accumulation of RNAs normally degraded as NMD substrates.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased levels of predicted NMD substrates.

claim: DUX4 mRNA is itself degraded by NMD.
source: DUX4 mRNA is itself degraded by NMD, such that inhibition of NMD by DUX4 protein stabilizes DUX4 mRNA through a double-negative feedback loop in FSHD muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased DUX4 mRNA levels following UPF1 knockdown.

claim: Inhibition of NMD by DUX4 protein stabilizes DUX4 mRNA through a double-negative feedback loop in FSHD muscle cells.
source: DUX4 mRNA is itself degraded by NMD, such that inhibition of NMD by DUX4 protein stabilizes DUX4 mRNA through a double-negative feedback loop in FSHD muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased endogenous DUX4 mRNA following ectopic DUX4 expression.

claim: The feedback loop between DUX4 and NMD is consistent with 'bursts' of DUX4 expression in FSHD muscle.
source: This feedback loop illustrates an unexpected mode of autoregulatory behavior of a transcription factor, is consistent with 'bursts' of DUX4 expression in FSHD muscle, and has implications for FSHD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the feedback loop mechanism and known DUX4 expression patterns.

claim: FSHD is typically an adult-onset muscular dystrophy characterized by muscle weakness initially affecting the face, shoulders, and upper arms.
source: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is typically an adult-onset muscular dystrophy characterized by muscle weakness initially affecting the face (facio), shoulders (scapulo), and upper arms (humeral).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about FSHD.

claim: FSHD is caused by decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in the subtelomeric region of chromosome 4q.
source: FSHD is caused by decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in the subtelomeric region of chromosome 4q, due to either D4Z4 repeat contractions (Lemmers et al., 2010) or mutations affecting trans-acting epigenetic regulators of the D4Z4 repeat such as SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012), which results in the misexpression of DUX4 mRNA in skeletal muscle and possibly other somatic tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: D4Z4 repeat contractions can cause decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array.
source: FSHD is caused by decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in the subtelomeric region of chromosome 4q, due to either D4Z4 repeat contractions (Lemmers et al., 2010) or mutations affecting trans-acting epigenetic regulators of the D4Z4 repeat such as SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012), which results in the misexpression of DUX4 mRNA in skeletal muscle and possibly other somatic tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations affecting SMCHD1 can cause decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array.
source: FSHD is caused by decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in the subtelomeric region of chromosome 4q, due to either D4Z4 repeat contractions (Lemmers et al., 2010) or mutations affecting trans-acting epigenetic regulators of the D4Z4 repeat such as SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012), which results in the misexpression of DUX4 mRNA in skeletal muscle and possibly other somatic tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lemmers et al., 2012.

claim: Decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 array results in the misexpression of DUX4 mRNA in skeletal muscle and possibly other somatic tissues.
source: FSHD is caused by decreased epigenetic repression of the D4Z4 macrosatellite array in the subtelomeric region of chromosome 4q, due to either D4Z4 repeat contractions (Lemmers et al., 2010) or mutations affecting trans-acting epigenetic regulators of the D4Z4 repeat such as SMCHD1 (Lemmers et al., 2012), which results in the misexpression of DUX4 mRNA in skeletal muscle and possibly other somatic tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FSHD pathogenesis.

claim: DUX4 activates germline genes and repetitive elements.
source: DUX4 encodes a double homeobox transcription factor that activates germline genes and repetitive elements (Geng et al., 2012) and causes apoptosis and atrophic myotube formation when misexpressed in skeletal muscle (Kowaljow et al., 2007; Vanderplanck et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2011; Mitsuhashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geng et al., 2012.

claim: DUX4 causes apoptosis and atrophic myotube formation when misexpressed in skeletal muscle.
source: DUX4 encodes a double homeobox transcription factor that activates germline genes and repetitive elements (Geng et al., 2012) and causes apoptosis and atrophic myotube formation when misexpressed in skeletal muscle (Kowaljow et al., 2007; Vanderplanck et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2011; Mitsuhashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: DUX4 is expressed in only a small fraction of nuclei.
source: DUX4 is expressed in only a small fraction of nuclei (Snider et al., 2010), likely due to occasional 'bursts' of DUX4 expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snider et al., 2010.

claim: The variegated expression of DUX4 is likely due to occasional 'bursts' of DUX4 expression.
source: DUX4 is expressed in only a small fraction of nuclei (Snider et al., 2010), likely due to occasional 'bursts' of DUX4 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression pattern.

claim: DUX4 expression results in increased abundance of many coding RNA isoforms containing premature translation termination codons upstream of splice junctions.
source: Further analysis of this data showed that DUX4 expression also resulted in the increased abundance of many coding RNA isoforms containing premature translation termination codons upstream of splice junctions.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: An isoform of the SRSF3 gene containing a well-characterized NMD-inducing cassette exon was present at low levels prior to DUX4 expression but became the dominant isoform thereafter in both 54-1 and MB135 cells.
source: For example, an isoform of the SRSF3 gene containing a well-characterized NMD-inducing cassette exon (Lareau et al., 2007; Ni et al., 2007) was present at low levels prior to DUX4 expression but became the dominant isoform thereafter in both 54-1 and MB135 cells (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A-B and citations to previous studies characterizing the cassette exon.

claim: Relative levels of the β-globin NMD substrate were twofold higher in DUX4-expressing vs control myoblasts.
source: Relative levels of the β-globin NMD substrate were twofold higher in DUX4-expressing vs control myoblasts, indicating that NMD is indeed compromised by DUX4 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the β-globin reporter assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NMD is compromised by DUX4.
source: Relative levels of the β-globin NMD substrate were twofold higher in DUX4-expressing vs control myoblasts, indicating that NMD is indeed compromised by DUX4 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased levels of NMD substrates in DUX4-expressing cells.

claim: Approximately 13% of predicted NMD substrates from cassette exon splicing events increased following DUX4 expression in 54-1 cells.
source: Restricting to cassette exon splicing events where one isoform, but not both, was a predicted NMD substrate, we found that ∼13% of such predicted NMD substrates increased following DUX4 expression, while ∼1.6% decreased, in 54-1 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Approximately 1.6% of predicted NMD substrates from cassette exon splicing events decreased following DUX4 expression in 54-1 cells.
source: Restricting to cassette exon splicing events where one isoform, but not both, was a predicted NMD substrate, we found that ∼13% of such predicted NMD substrates increased following DUX4 expression, while ∼1.6% decreased, in 54-1 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Impaired NMD causes accumulation of aberrant mRNAs resulting from mis-splicing or incomplete splicing.
source: Impaired NMD also caused accumulation of aberrant mRNAs resulting from mis-splicing or incomplete splicing, which are common byproducts of the stochastic nature of the splicing process (Weischenfeldt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weischenfeldt et al., 2012 and experimental data.

claim: Approximately 13% of annotated constitutive junctions exhibited increased aberrant splicing in DUX4-expressing vs control cells.
source: We identified and quantified alternative splicing of annotated constitutive junctions, finding that ∼13% of such junctions exhibited increased aberrant splicing in DUX4-expressing vs control cells, while only ∼0.25% exhibited decreased aberrant splicing (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only approximately 0.25% of annotated constitutive junctions exhibited decreased aberrant splicing in DUX4-expressing vs control cells.
source: We identified and quantified alternative splicing of annotated constitutive junctions, finding that ∼13% of such junctions exhibited increased aberrant splicing in DUX4-expressing vs control cells, while only ∼0.25% exhibited decreased aberrant splicing (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The vast majority of novel products of annotated constitutive junctions were present at very low or undetectable levels in control 54-1 myoblasts.
source: The vast majority of these novel products of annotated constitutive junctions were present at very low or undetectable levels in control 54-1 myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: DUX4 expression caused increased levels of predicted NMD substrates for all classes of splicing events in both 54-1 and MB135 cells.
source: We next extended this analysis to all classes of splicing events, including mis-splicing and intron retention of constitutive splice junctions. DUX4 expression caused increased levels of predicted NMD substrates for all classes of splicing events in both 54-1 and MB135 cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The increases in NMD substrates were generally more extreme in 54-1 than in MB135 cells.
source: These increases were generally more extreme in 54-1 than in MB135 cells, likely due to the ∼15-fold higher DUX4 expression achieved in 54-1 vs MB135 cells as well as the longer time period allowed for infection (48 hr vs 24 hr).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and experimental conditions.

claim: The more extreme increases in NMD substrates in 54-1 cells are likely due to the approximately 15-fold higher DUX4 expression achieved in 54-1 vs MB135 cells and the longer time period allowed for infection.
source: These increases were generally more extreme in 54-1 than in MB135 cells, likely due to the ∼15-fold higher DUX4 expression achieved in 54-1 vs MB135 cells as well as the longer time period allowed for infection (48 hr vs 24 hr).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental conditions and observed results.

claim: High levels of NMD substrates in DUX4-expressing cells were not simply a side effect of DUX4-induced apoptosis.
source: High levels of NMD substrates in DUX4-expressing cells were not simply a side effect of DUX4-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that TP53 knockdown prevented apoptosis but not NMD inhibition.

claim: TP53 knock-down prevented apoptosis following DUX4 expression in normal myoblasts.
source: TP53 knock-down (KD) prevented apoptosis following DUX4 expression in normal myoblasts, confirming previous reports that DUX4 toxicity is p53-dependent (Wallace et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Wallace et al., 2011.

claim: DUX4 toxicity is p53-dependent.
source: TP53 knock-down (KD) prevented apoptosis following DUX4 expression in normal myoblasts, confirming previous reports that DUX4 toxicity is p53-dependent (Wallace et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wallace et al., 2011 and experimental data.

claim: TP53 KD did not prevent DUX4-induced NMD inhibition.
source: However, TP53 KD did not prevent DUX4-induced NMD inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No UPF or SMG NMD factors exhibited decreased mRNA levels following DUX4 expression.
source: However, no UPF or SMG NMD factors exhibited decreased mRNA levels following DUX4 expression, and most were up-regulated by two- to fourfold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most UPF or SMG NMD factors were up-regulated by two- to fourfold following DUX4 expression.
source: However, no UPF or SMG NMD factors exhibited decreased mRNA levels following DUX4 expression, and most were up-regulated by two- to fourfold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mRNA levels of most NMD factors increase following the knock-down of UPF1.
source: This expression pattern was reminiscent of a recent report that mRNA levels of most NMD factors increase following the knock-down of UPF1, encoding a central component of the NMD machinery (Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2011.

claim: UPF1 protein levels were markedly lower in DUX4-expressing myoblasts than in control myoblasts.
source: UPF1 protein levels were markedly lower in DUX4-expressing myoblasts than in control myoblasts, as were SMG7 levels, although to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SMG7 protein levels were lower in DUX4-expressing myoblasts than in control myoblasts, although to a lesser extent than UPF1.
source: UPF1 protein levels were markedly lower in DUX4-expressing myoblasts than in control myoblasts, as were SMG7 levels, although to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: UPF3B protein levels were unaffected by DUX4 expression.
source: In contrast, UPF3B levels were unaffected by DUX4 expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DUX4 was robustly detectable 12–14 hr after lentiviral infection.
source: DUX4 was robustly detectable 12–14 hr after lentiviral infection, coincident with the beginning of a sharp decrease in UPF1 levels (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The beginning of a sharp decrease in UPF1 levels was coincident with DUX4 becoming robustly detectable 12–14 hr after lentiviral infection.
source: DUX4 was robustly detectable 12–14 hr after lentiviral infection, coincident with the beginning of a sharp decrease in UPF1 levels (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: SMG7 showed a more modest decrease through the time course compared to UPF1.
source: SMG7 showed a more modest decrease through the time course, while UPF3B levels were relatively constant.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: UPF3B levels were relatively constant through the time course.
source: SMG7 showed a more modest decrease through the time course, while UPF3B levels were relatively constant.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NMD substrates produced from the β-globin reporter exhibited increased levels 12–14 hr after lentiviral expression.
source: NMD substrates produced from the β-globin reporter, as well as endogenously produced from the SRSF2 and SRSF3 genes, exhibited increased levels 12–14 hr after lentiviral expression (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: NMD substrates endogenously produced from the SRSF2 and SRSF3 genes exhibited increased levels 12–14 hr after lentiviral expression.
source: NMD substrates produced from the β-globin reporter, as well as endogenously produced from the SRSF2 and SRSF3 genes, exhibited increased levels 12–14 hr after lentiviral expression (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The close temporal coupling between DUX4 protein production, decreased UPF1 levels, and increased levels of both endogenous and exogenous NMD substrates suggests that insufficient levels of UPF1 may contribute to inefficient NMD in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: The close temporal coupling between DUX4 protein production, decreased UPF1 levels, and increased levels of both endogenous and exogenous NMD substrates suggests that insufficient levels of UPF1—and perhaps additional NMD machinery components such as SMG7—may contribute to inefficient NMD in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation observed in the time course experiments.

claim: Insufficient levels of SMG7 may contribute to inefficient NMD in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: The close temporal coupling between DUX4 protein production, decreased UPF1 levels, and increased levels of both endogenous and exogenous NMD substrates suggests that insufficient levels of UPF1—and perhaps additional NMD machinery components such as SMG7—may contribute to inefficient NMD in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed SMG7 decrease.

claim: The rapid decrease in UPF1 levels suggests that DUX4 might trigger UPF1 degradation.
source: The rapid decrease in UPF1 levels that we observed suggested that DUX4 might trigger UPF1 degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed rapid decrease in UPF1 protein levels.

claim: MG132 treatment restored normal UPF1 levels in DUX4-expressing myoblasts.
source: MG132 treatment restored normal UPF1 levels in DUX4-expressing myoblasts, while UPF1 levels in control myoblasts were unaffected (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: UPF1 levels in control myoblasts were unaffected by MG132 treatment.
source: MG132 treatment restored normal UPF1 levels in DUX4-expressing myoblasts, while UPF1 levels in control myoblasts were unaffected (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The close temporal relationship between the onset of decreased UPF1 levels and increased NMD substrates strongly suggests that UPF1 degradation contributes to NMD inhibition in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: However, the close temporal relationship between the onset of decreased UPF1 levels and increased NMD substrates strongly suggests that UPF1 degradation contributes to NMD inhibition in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation observed in experiments.

claim: Both DUX4 isoforms encoding the full-length protein contain a constitutively spliced intron within their 3′ UTRs.
source: Both DUX4 isoforms encoding the full-length protein contain a constitutively spliced intron within their 3′ UTRs, rendering them likely NMD substrates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The constitutively spliced intron within the 3′ UTRs of DUX4 isoforms renders them likely NMD substrates.
source: Both DUX4 isoforms encoding the full-length protein contain a constitutively spliced intron within their 3′ UTRs, rendering them likely NMD substrates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on known NMD rules and the structure of DUX4 mRNA.

claim: UPF1 was knocked down to 24.3% of normal protein levels in 54-2 myoblasts.
source: We knocked down UFP1 in 54-2 and MB200 myoblasts to 24.3% and 32.4% of normal protein levels, respectively, and differentiated these myoblasts to myotubes to stimulate DUX4 transcription.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: UPF1 was knocked down to 32.4% of normal protein levels in MB200 myoblasts.
source: We knocked down UFP1 in 54-2 and MB200 myoblasts to 24.3% and 32.4% of normal protein levels, respectively, and differentiated these myoblasts to myotubes to stimulate DUX4 transcription.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: DUX4 mRNA was expressed at approximately fourfold higher levels in UPF1 KD vs control KD myotubes.
source: DUX4 mRNA was expressed at approximately fourfold higher levels in UPF1 KD vs control KD myotubes, as was ZSCAN4 mRNA, which is transcriptionally activated by DUX4 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZSCAN4 mRNA was expressed at approximately fourfold higher levels in UPF1 KD vs control KD myotubes.
source: DUX4 mRNA was expressed at approximately fourfold higher levels in UPF1 KD vs control KD myotubes, as was ZSCAN4 mRNA, which is transcriptionally activated by DUX4 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ZSCAN4 is transcriptionally activated by DUX4.
source: DUX4 mRNA was expressed at approximately fourfold higher levels in UPF1 KD vs control KD myotubes, as was ZSCAN4 mRNA, which is transcriptionally activated by DUX4 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Transcripts from the chimeric construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased twofold following UPF1 KD in normal myoblasts.
source: Transcripts from the chimeric construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased twofold following UPF1 KD in normal myoblasts—a substantial but smaller increase than we observed for the endogenous DUX4 mRNA, perhaps due to the chimeric nature of the β-globin + DUX4 3′ UTR construct—while transcripts from the construct lacking the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR increased only 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Transcripts from the construct lacking the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR increased only 1.5-fold following UPF1 KD in normal myoblasts.
source: Transcripts from the chimeric construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased twofold following UPF1 KD in normal myoblasts—a substantial but smaller increase than we observed for the endogenous DUX4 mRNA, perhaps due to the chimeric nature of the β-globin + DUX4 3′ UTR construct—while transcripts from the construct lacking the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR increased only 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR is important for NMD-induced degradation of the DUX4 mRNA.
source: We conclude that the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR is important for NMD-induced degradation of the DUX4 mRNA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response of constructs with and without the second intron to UPF1 KD.

claim: DUX4 exhibits variegated expression in FSHD muscle cells, with only a few percent of nuclei detectable as DUX4+.
source: DUX4 exhibits variegated expression in FSHD muscle cells, with only a few percent of nuclei detectable as DUX4+ (Snider et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snider et al., 2010.

claim: The fraction of DUX4+ nuclei increased from 0.3% to 2.1% following UPF1 KD in FSHD myotubes.
source: Immunostaining of FSHD myotubes revealed that the fraction of DUX4+ nuclei increased from 0.3% to 2.1% following UPF1 KD, a substantial order-of-magnitude increase (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: NMD is an endogenous suppressor of DUX4 mRNA levels that contributes to the very low and variegated expression of DUX4.
source: Together, our data show that NMD is an endogenous suppressor of DUX4 mRNA levels that contributes to the very low and variegated expression of DUX4, a characteristic feature of FSHD muscle cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased DUX4 expression following NMD inhibition.

claim: Ectopic DUX4 expression led to an approximately fivefold increase in endogenously transcribed DUX4 mRNA levels.
source: To test this, we ectopically expressed DUX4 in FSHD1 and FSHD2 myotubes and measured levels of endogenously transcribed DUX4 mRNA. Ectopic DUX4 expression led to an approximately fivefold increase in endogenously transcribed DUX4 mRNA levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Levels of the NMD-susceptible construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased 1.43-fold following ectopic DUX4 expression.
source: Levels of the NMD-susceptible construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased 1.43-fold following ectopic DUX4 expression, while levels of the construct without the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR exhibited a more modest increase of 1.08-fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Levels of the construct without the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR exhibited a more modest increase of 1.08-fold following ectopic DUX4 expression.
source: Levels of the NMD-susceptible construct containing the complete DUX4 3′ UTR increased 1.43-fold following ectopic DUX4 expression, while levels of the construct without the second intron of the DUX4 3′ UTR exhibited a more modest increase of 1.08-fold (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The DUX4 3′ UTR targets DUX4 mRNA for NMD.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that the DUX4 3′ UTR targets DUX4 mRNA for NMD and that DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD results in increased perdurance of the DUX4 mRNA as a possible mechanism of positive autoregulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from UPF1 KD and chimeric construct experiments.

claim: DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD results in increased perdurance of the DUX4 mRNA as a possible mechanism of positive autoregulation.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that the DUX4 3′ UTR targets DUX4 mRNA for NMD and that DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD results in increased perdurance of the DUX4 mRNA as a possible mechanism of positive autoregulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the feedback loop.

claim: The NMD-mediated autoregulation mechanism might contribute to the spreading of DUX4 expression between adjacent nuclei in a muscle fiber.
source: However, it is interesting to consider that this mechanism might contribute to the spreading of DUX4 expression between adjacent nuclei in a muscle fiber.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological implications.

claim: Muscle fibers contain arrays of closely spaced nuclei.
source: Because muscle fibers contain arrays of closely spaced nuclei, the expression of DUX4 mRNA from one nucleus will distribute protein to the surrounding nuclei and induce a region of NMD inhibition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle fiber structure.

claim: The expression of DUX4 mRNA from one nucleus will distribute protein to the surrounding nuclei and induce a region of NMD inhibition.
source: Because muscle fibers contain arrays of closely spaced nuclei, the expression of DUX4 mRNA from one nucleus will distribute protein to the surrounding nuclei and induce a region of NMD inhibition.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed mechanism and muscle fiber structure.

claim: DUX4-mediated degradation of UPF1 contributes to DUX4-induced NMD inhibition.
source: The close temporal coupling between the onset of DUX4 expression, decreases in UPF1 protein, and increases in NMD substrates (Figure 2) strongly suggests that DUX4-mediated degradation of UPF1 contributes to DUX4-induced NMD inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation observed in experiments.

claim: UPF1 proteolysis constitutes a potential new regulator of cellular NMD efficiency.
source: Nonetheless, as we are unaware of other reports of physiological stimuli triggering rapid UPF1 protein degradation, our data suggest that UPF1 proteolysis constitutes a potential new regulator of cellular NMD efficiency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the novelty of the observed mechanism.

claim: Many of the most up-regulated genes following DUX4 expression in normal myoblasts are involved in the ubiquitin–proteasome system, including numerous E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: We previously observed that many of the most up-regulated genes following DUX4 expression in normal myoblasts are involved in the ubiquitin–proteasome system, including numerous E3 ubiquitin ligases (Geng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geng et al., 2012.

claim: DUX4-induced dysregulation of the ubiquitin–proteasome system may be responsible for triggering UPF1 protein degradation.
source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that DUX4-induced dysregulation of the ubiquitin–proteasome system is responsible for triggering UPF1 protein degradation.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed gene expression changes.

claim: DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD may contribute to FSHD pathophysiology through both cell autonomous and non-cell autonomous mechanisms.
source: DUX4-mediated inhibition of NMD may contribute to FSHD pathophysiology through both cell autonomous and non-cell autonomous mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about potential disease mechanisms.

claim: The accumulation of abnormal RNAs may cause direct or indirect toxic effects in muscle cells due to intrinsic toxicity of abnormal RNAs or a stress response to the production of abnormal proteins.
source: The accumulation of abnormal RNAs may cause direct or indirect toxic effects in muscle cells due to intrinsic toxicity of abnormal RNAs or a stress response to the production of abnormal proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of toxicity.

claim: FSHD muscle is frequently characterized by a T-cell infiltrate.
source: FSHD muscle is frequently characterized by a T-cell infiltrate (Arahata et al., 1995), and it is possible that stabilized NMD substrates encode novel peptides with antigenic potential, contributing to an immune response (Pastor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arahata et al., 1995.

claim: Stabilized NMD substrates may encode novel peptides with antigenic potential, contributing to an immune response.
source: FSHD muscle is frequently characterized by a T-cell infiltrate (Arahata et al., 1995), and it is possible that stabilized NMD substrates encode novel peptides with antigenic potential, contributing to an immune response (Pastor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Pastor et al., 2010.

claim: Production of antigenic peptides could potentially enable even a small fraction of DUX4+ nuclei to induce widespread pathology within a muscle fiber.
source: Production of antigenic peptides could potentially enable even a small fraction of DUX4+ nuclei to induce widespread pathology within a muscle fiber.
evidence: This is speculation about potential disease mechanisms.

claim: The degree of NMD inhibition induced by DUX4 is comparable to that observed in previous studies involving genetic ablation of components of the NMD machinery.
source: Consistent with the idea that NMD inhibition may contribute to DUX4 toxicity in skeletal muscle, it is interesting to note that the degree of NMD inhibition induced by DUX4 is comparable to that observed in previous studies involving genetic ablation of components of the NMD machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with published data.

claim: A study of mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking Smg1 found that 9% of predicted NMD substrates created by alternative splicing exhibited increased levels relative to wild-type cells.
source: For example, a recent study of mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking Smg1, which encodes a kinase responsible for phosphorylating UPF1, found that 9% of predicted NMD substrates created by alternative splicing exhibited increased levels relative to wild-type cells (McIlwain et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McIlwain et al., 2010.

claim: DUX4-induced NMD inhibition causes profoundly abnormal RNA metabolism.
source: In comparison, we found that 13% of such substrates were up-regulated following DUX4 expression (Figure 1), suggesting that DUX4-induced NMD inhibition causes profoundly abnormal RNA metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the magnitude of NMD inhibition.

claim: RNA toxicity is the major pathophysiologic mechanism in myotonic dystrophy.
source: As RNA toxicity is the major pathophysiologic mechanism in myotonic dystrophy, it is interesting to consider that RNA-mediated disease mechanisms may also have important roles in FSHD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myotonic dystrophy.

claim: RNA-mediated disease mechanisms may have important roles in FSHD.
source: As RNA toxicity is the major pathophysiologic mechanism in myotonic dystrophy, it is interesting to consider that RNA-mediated disease mechanisms may also have important roles in FSHD.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy with myotonic dystrophy.

claim: The SRSF3 gene contains a well-characterized NMD-inducing cassette exon.
source: For example, an isoform of the SRSF3 gene containing a well-characterized NMD-inducing cassette exon (Lareau et al., 2007; Ni et al., 2007) was present at low levels prior to DUX4 expression but became the dominant isoform thereafter in both 54-1 and MB135 cells (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lareau et al., 2007 and Ni et al., 2007.

claim: UPF1 is a central component of the NMD machinery.
source: We report that DUX4-triggered proteolytic degradation of UPF1, a central component of the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) machinery, is associated with profound NMD inhibition, resulting in global accumulation of RNAs normally degraded as NMD substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NMD pathway.

claim: Proteasome inhibition inhibits normal translation.
source: As proteasome inhibition inhibits normal translation (Cowan and Morley, 2004; Mazroui et al., 2007) and therefore NMD, we were unable to test whether the restoration of normal UPF1 levels by proteasomal inhibition rescued NMD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cowan and Morley, 2004 and Mazroui et al., 2007.

claim: Proteasome inhibition inhibits NMD.
source: As proteasome inhibition inhibits normal translation (Cowan and Morley, 2004; Mazroui et al., 2007) and therefore NMD, we were unable to test whether the restoration of normal UPF1 levels by proteasomal inhibition rescued NMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between translation and NMD, supported by citations.

claim: The second intron of DUX4's 3′ UTR lies 100 nt downstream of the termination codon.
source: We focused on the constitutively spliced second intron within the 3′ UTR because it lies 100 nt downstream of the termination codon, and therefore it is predicted to trigger NMD.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the DUX4 gene.

claim: An intron lying 100 nt downstream of the termination codon is predicted to trigger NMD.
source: We focused on the constitutively spliced second intron within the 3′ UTR because it lies 100 nt downstream of the termination codon, and therefore it is predicted to trigger NMD.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NMD rules.

claim: 54-2 cells are isogenic to normal 54-1 cells but carry a contracted D4Z4 array.
source: To test this, we used cells isolated from FSHD1 (54-2, which are isogenic to normal 54-1 cells but carry a contracted D4Z4 array) and FSHD2 (MB200) skeletal muscle (Krom et al., 2012; Schoenberg and Maquat, 2012; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the cell lines.

claim: Histone H3 has a long half-life.
source: Loading control H3, histone 3, has a long half-life (Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Toyama et al., 2013.
